title: Prompt Engineering for Claude
description: Learn Claude-specific prompting techniques that produce consistently better results — from basic structure to advanced patterns.

data.text: Prompt engineering for Claude is less about 'tricking' the model and more about clear communication. Claude responds to structure, context, and specificity the same way a skilled human would. The better you are at expressing what you need — and why — the better Claude's output will be.

data.title: Principles that work especially well with Claude:
items: Be explicit about role — tell Claude who it should 'be' for this task
Provide examples — showing Claude what you want is more effective than describing it
Use XML tags to structure complex prompts — Claude understands them well
Specify output format — ask for bullet points, tables, JSON, etc.
Give Claude reasoning tasks — ask it to 'think through' complex problems
Set constraints — 'respond in under 200 words', 'avoid jargon', 'use only sources I provide'

data.text: Claude responds exceptionally well to XML tags in prompts. You can wrap different parts of your prompt in tags like <instructions>, <context>, <example>, <output_format>, and <constraints>. This structure helps Claude parse your request correctly and produces more consistent, reliable output.

data.title: XML-structured prompt
data.content:
<instructions>
You are a senior product manager writing a PRD. Write a clear, structured product requirements document.
</instructions>

<context>
We are building a feature that lets users save AI conversations to Notion. Users have been asking for this for 6 months. The engineering team is ready to start in Q1.
</context>

<output_format>
Use these sections: Problem, Solution, User Stories, Success Metrics, Risks, Timeline.
</output_format>

<constraints>
Keep it under 800 words. Use bullet points for user stories. Do not include implementation details.
</constraints>

data.text: Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting asks Claude to show its reasoning before giving a final answer. This is especially effective for complex analysis, math problems, or decisions with multiple factors. Claude's responses are more accurate when it is asked to 'think step by step' or 'show your reasoning'.

data.title: Chain of thought example
data.content:
Prompt: 'I'm deciding between two job offers. Can you help me think through this?

Offer A: $120K, remote, startup, less stable
Offer B: $100K, hybrid, Fortune 500, very stable

Before giving a recommendation, walk through the key factors I should consider: compensation total value, career growth, stability, work-life balance, and alignment with my goals. Show your reasoning for each factor.'

Claude will produce a more thoughtful, structured analysis when asked to reason first.

data.text: Few-shot prompting means giving Claude examples of the output you want before asking for new output. This is one of the most powerful techniques for getting consistent formatting and style. Show Claude 2-3 examples of what good looks like, and it will match that pattern reliably.

data.title: Few-shot prompting for consistent format
data.content:
Prompt: 'Here are two examples of how I want meeting notes formatted. Follow this exact format for any new meeting notes I provide.'

Example 1:
Date: [date]
Attendees: [names]
Key Decisions: [bullet list]
Action Items: [bullet list with owner]

Example 2:
[Same format]

'Now format these new meeting notes: [paste notes]'

data.title: A repeatable prompt engineering workflow:
items: Start with a clear, simple prompt
Test it and note what is wrong with the output
Identify the specific issue: wrong format? Wrong tone? Missing context?
Revise the prompt to address that specific issue
Once it works for one input, test on 2-3 more variations

data.caption: The iterative prompt engineering cycle
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  A[Write Initial Prompt] --> B[Test Output]
  B --> C[Identify Issue]
  C --> D[Revise Prompt]
  D --> B
  B -->|Works| E[Test Variations]
  E --> F[Refined Prompt]

data.title: Mistakes to avoid:
items: Being too vague — 'write something about marketing' produces generic output
Giving too many instructions at once — Claude misses details in long, unstructured prompts
Not specifying the output format — Claude will guess
Not providing examples when you need a specific format or style
Assuming Claude knows your context — always provide background information
Not iterating — the first prompt is rarely the best prompt

data.title: The test-and-refine method
data.text: The most effective prompt engineers are not the ones who write perfect prompts on the first try. They are the ones who test quickly, identify what is wrong, and refine. Treat prompt engineering like design: iterate fast, test often, and measure results by output quality.

data.title: Prompt engineering for Claude
points: Use XML tags to structure complex prompts clearly
Chain of Thought improves reasoning and complex analysis
Few-shot prompting with examples produces consistent formatting
Iterate: test, identify issues, refine, repeat
Specify output format, tone, and constraints explicitly
